title: Mac keyboard shortcuts I keep forgetting: why it happens and free fixes for developers
metaTitle: Mac Keyboard Shortcuts I Keep Forgetting: Causes and Free Fixes
description: Forgetting Mac keyboard shortcuts is a memory problem, not a flaw. See why it happens, what it costs developers, and free fixes that stick.
targetKeyword: mac keyboard shortcuts i keep forgetting
secondaryKeywords: see keyboard shortcuts in mac app
intro: You forget Mac keyboard shortcuts because they hide in menus, change from app to app, and fade when you stop using them. The fix is to see each one often, learn a few at a time, and add your own for the commands you reach for most. This page covers the causes, the cost, and free fixes that use Apple's own settings.
tldr: Most shortcuts are not on a poster. They sit in menus, and the menu is your reminder.
Shortcuts often differ between apps, so learn them per app, starting with the one you open most.
Forgetting is a memory problem. A few shortcuts practiced over several days is easier to keep than one long session.
System Settings lets you add shortcuts for menu commands that have none.
Lazur can point at a menu item and answer questions about the screen out loud. It does not press keys for you.

blocks.text: Why Mac shortcuts slip out of your head

Mac shortcuts are not one set. Apple's help page says a shortcut that works in one app might not work in another. Apple lists copy, paste, undo, and switching apps as basic shortcuts. Most other commands belong to the app you are in. You learn a key in your editor, then open a browser where the same keys do nothing. That split is the first reason the memory breaks.

The basic set is short. ⌘C copies, ⌘V pastes, ⌘Z undoes, ⇧⌘Z redoes, ⌘Space opens Spotlight, and ⌘Tab switches to the app you used most recently. Those six keys cover many small moments in a day. The gap is in the long tail. That means the commands you use twice a month, like Find in a specific tool or a tab command in your browser. Those are the ones that fade first, because you rarely give them a chance to repeat.
What the evidence does and does not show

I looked for a survey that counts how many people forget Mac shortcuts. I did not find one. So this page does not claim how common the problem is. The research I could open is narrower. Murre and Dros (2015, PLOS ONE) replicated Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve. Their only subject was one person, who spent 70 hours learning and relearning lists. Retention was measured from 20 minutes to 31 days. That shows the shape of forgetting in one memory. It does not measure a typical developer.

items: Apple's shortcut pages: which keys are built in, and how to add shortcuts for menu commands.

blocks.text: What forgetting costs a developer

Treat the cost as a rough estimate, not a verdict. The BLS reports a median annual wage of $135,980 for software developers in May 2025. Divide that by about 2,080 paid hours and you get roughly $65 an hour. Now say shortcut gaps cost you 10 minutes a week, mostly from searching menus. Over 48 to 50 working weeks, that comes to roughly $520 to $545 a year. Those inputs are assumptions. Change them and the total moves.

Example input, replace with your own

blocks.text: Use your own numbers. Count how many times this week you opened a menu for a command you already knew. Multiply by the seconds each one took. Then add a guess for the lost thread after each detour. That total comes from your own week, which is more useful than a general average. If your count is ten detours a day at five seconds each, that is less than a minute a day. The bigger cost is the thought you lose when you stop typing to hunt for a command.
A worked example in your editor and browser

Say you spend an hour in Cursor or VS Code. You open files, run a terminal, and save often. These are the default Mac shortcuts in VS Code. ⌘P opens Quick Open for a file name. ⇧⌘P opens the Command Palette, where each command has a name you can type. ⌃` toggles the integrated terminal. ⌘B toggles the sidebar. Cursor and VS Code share many menus, but your Cursor keys can differ, so open its Keyboard Shortcuts editor and check. The [Cursor guide](/for/developers/cursor) and the [VS Code guide](/for/developers/vs-code) go deeper.

items: Xcode: ⌘B builds, ⌘R runs, and ⌘U runs tests.
Slack: ⌘K opens the quick switcher, so you can jump to a channel or person.
Chrome: ⌘T opens a new tab, ⇧⌘T reopens the last closed tab, and ⌘L moves focus to the address bar.

blocks.text: These are defaults. If you or your team changed them, your keys differ. Open the menu bar and read the symbols to confirm. Trust the menu over any list, including this one. A list can be right last year and wrong after one settings change.
How to read shortcuts from menus instead of memorizing them

Every Mac app shows its shortcuts beside its menu items. Open File, Edit, or View and look at the right side of each command. The symbols give you the keys. ⌘ is Command, ⌥ is Option, ⌃ is Control, and ⇧ is Shift. Apple's page explains this layout. It does not say that holding Command reveals shortcuts, so do not count on that trick.

Reading the menu is a small habit with a big payoff. Each time you open a menu, glance at the right edge before you click. Say the key once under your breath. Do this for five commands a day and the keys start to stick, because you saw them in the place you needed them.
Add shortcuts for menu commands you use every day

items: Open System Settings.
Go to Keyboard > Keyboard Shortcuts, then select App Shortcuts.
Add a new entry for the app you want to change.
Type the exact menu item name, spelled and capitalized as it appears in the menu.
Press the key combination you want, then test it in the app.

blocks.text: The name must match exactly. If the menu says Reload This Page, type that. A close guess does nothing. Pick a combination that no menu already uses. If you choose one a menu already owns, you create a clash to sort out. Test each new shortcut in the app before you rely on it. Start with one entry. Two or three is plenty for the first month.
When a shortcut does nothing or does the wrong thing

items: The app is not frontmost. Click its window, then press the keys again.
The shortcut belongs to another app. Open that app's menus and check.
A system shortcut took the keys. Look in System Settings > Keyboard > Keyboard Shortcuts for the clash.
A key remap changed the key. Check any keyboard tool you installed.

blocks.text: Some mistakes are costly. Command-Q quits the whole app, not just the window. Command-W closes only the front window. Learn both on purpose, because the wrong one can end more work than you meant to. If a shortcut seems to do nothing, check the menu before you press it again. Pressing a key twice can run the command twice.
Viewing shortcuts without memorizing every one

KeyCue is a Mac app that displays the keyboard shortcuts of the frontmost app. The Ergonis download page lists version 11.2.1, dated Aug 3, 2026, and a requirement of macOS 13 or later. The page offers a free download and a Buy now button. It does not state a price, so check the Ergonis site before you pay.

Other shortcut viewers exist. I did not verify their current status or prices, so check the developer's own site before you install one. A viewer helps most when you forget a key in the middle of work and do not want to stop and search.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a command is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it on your screen. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.

Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. It is not a plugin for any app. That makes it a guide while you learn. It does not replace the learning. Keep your hands on the keys, and use Lazur when you are stuck on where a command lives.
Privacy and client code on your screen

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer your question. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models. Read those terms on the site before you rely on them.

Before you hold the shortcut on a screen with client code, customer records, or patient data, check your employer's rules. If you work in a regulated job, follow your employer's rules on client or patient data first. Your employer decides what can appear on a screen Lazur reads.
Mistakes people make while memorizing shortcuts

items: Learning a long list in one sitting. Pick the few commands you use each week and stop there.
Learning shortcuts you never use. Start with commands that show up in your daily work.
Forgetting which app is in front. The same keys can mean different commands in each app.
Remapping keys before you know the defaults. Learn the default first, then change it.
Dropping the menu too soon. The menu is your reminder, so keep using it while you learn.

blocks.text: The most common mistake is treating a failed shortcut as a sign of a bad memory. Usually the app in front is not the one you think it is. Click the window you want, then try again. Most failures are focus problems, not forgetting.
Build a shortcut sheet you will actually open

Keep a short note, grouped by app, with only the commands you use every week. Put the menu path next to each key, such as Edit > Find. The path rescues you when the key slips. Review the note each Friday and remove anything you no longer use. If typing the note is slow, hold fn to dictate it straight into a text file.
Next steps for this week

items: Open the menus of your main app and read the symbols once.
Add one App Shortcut for a command you reach for with the mouse.
Check the menu first when a shortcut does not work, then ask Lazur if you are still stuck.
Look at the [pricing page](/pricing) only after you know whether daily voice help is worth it to you.

faq.question: Why do I forget Mac keyboard shortcuts so quickly?
faq.answer: Most shortcuts are used rarely, and many belong to one app only. Memory fades without reuse. A replication of Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve measured retention from 20 minutes to 31 days, but it had one subject. Treat it as a pattern, not proof about you.

faq.question: Which Mac shortcuts should I learn first?
faq.answer: Start with the basic set Apple lists: ⌘C, ⌘V, ⌘Z, ⇧⌘Z, ⌘Space, and ⌘Tab. Then add the three or four commands you repeat most in your main app.

faq.question: How do I see the shortcuts for the app I am using?
faq.answer: Open its menus. Each command shows its shortcut on the right. KeyCue is a third-party Mac app that displays the frontmost app's shortcuts, if you want a viewer.

faq.question: Can I change a Mac keyboard shortcut?
faq.answer: Yes, for many menu commands. Go to System Settings > Keyboard > Keyboard Shortcuts, select App Shortcuts, add an entry, and type the exact menu item name with the keys you choose.

faq.question: Why does a shortcut work in one app but not another?
faq.answer: Apple's help page says shortcuts that work in one app might not work in another. Each app builds its own menus, so the same keys can run a different command or nothing.

faq.question: Does KeyCue cost money?
faq.answer: The Ergonis download page offers a free download and a Buy now button, but it does not state a price. I could not confirm current pricing, so check the Ergonis site before you install.

faq.question: Can Lazur press shortcuts for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. It can point at a menu item, answer questions about the screen out loud, and guide you one click at a time.

faq.question: Is it safe to use Lazur on work code?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks only while you hold the shortcut. If your screen shows client code, customer data, or patient records, follow your employer's rules before you use it.

faq.question: Is there a way to try Lazur first?
faq.answer: Lazur offers a short Pro trial with no credit card. Check the [pricing page](/pricing) for current plans and what the trial includes.

faq.question: Should I use shortcuts or the mouse?
faq.answer: Use shortcuts for commands you repeat several times a day. Keep the mouse for rare commands. The goal is fewer moments of searching, not zero mouse use.

costs.title: Minutes lost to menu hunting
costs.text: Every time you open a menu for a command you already know, you spend seconds you did not need to spend. Those seconds add up over a week. The example above puts a rough figure on it: 10 minutes a week, or about $520 to $545 a year at a developer's median pay. Treat that as one estimate, not a fact about you.

costs.title: The lost thread after each detour
costs.text: Switching from the keys to the mouse changes what your hands are doing. You stop typing, search for the command, then come back. That gap is hard to measure, so this page does not put a number on it.

costs.title: Mistakes from the wrong key
costs.text: Command-Q quits the whole app, while Command-W closes one window. Pressing the wrong one by reflex can end more work than you intended. A slip like that costs time to reopen what you had open.

costs.title: Searching for an answer you already have
costs.text: Many people look up a shortcut on the web when the menu already shows it. A search takes a tab, a page load, and a scan of results. The menu takes one glance.

costs.title: Friction between Windows and Mac
costs.text: If you use Windows at work or at home, Control and Command swap roles in your hands. Your fingers reach for Control on the Mac. Copy and paste feel right, but they land on the wrong modifier until the habit changes.

causes.title: Shortcuts belong to each app
causes.text: Apple says a shortcut that works in one app might not work in another. Each app defines its own menus, so the same key can mean different commands. You learn a key once, then meet it again in a tool that uses it differently. That split weakens the memory because the cue is inconsistent.

causes.title: Memory fades without reuse
causes.text: The Murre and Dros replication used one person, so it does not tell you how fast a typical developer forgets. It does show the basic pattern. The study measured retention by relearning time after each interval. Shortcuts you touch once a month fall into that gap.

causes.title: The mouse is always visible
causes.text: Menus sit on screen, and the pointer is already in your hand. Reaching for the menu wins by default. A shortcut only takes over after you have used it enough times to make it automatic.

causes.title: Too many keys at once
causes.text: A long list learned in one sitting gives each shortcut little reuse. Without reuse, the memory fades fast. Fewer keys with more repetition is a better trade.

causes.title: Switching apps all day
causes.text: Developers move between an editor, a terminal, a browser, chat, and an issue tracker many times a day. Each switch changes which shortcuts are live. Holding several sets at once is where mistakes start.

causes.title: Customized or remapped keys
causes.text: Some Macs have remapped keys, and some teams change defaults. Your shortcut may not match a guide written for stock settings. Check your keyboard settings before you blame your memory.

fixes.title: Read the symbols on purpose
fixes.text: When you use a menu with the mouse, read the shortcut beside the command. Say it out loud if that helps. Then press the keys next time instead of clicking. The first try is slow. Repetition makes it faster.

fixes.title: Learn a few per app, one app at a time
fixes.text: Choose one app. Pick three commands you use weekly. Practice them for a few days, then add three more. A small set you use often beats a long list you read once.

fixes.title: Add App Shortcuts for your own favorites
fixes.text: Use System Settings > Keyboard > Keyboard Shortcuts > App Shortcuts to give a menu command a key you can remember. Pick a combination that matches a pattern you already use. Type the exact menu name, then test it right away.

fixes.title: Use the Command Palette in your editor
fixes.text: In VS Code and Cursor, ⇧⌘P opens the Command Palette. Type what you want, such as toggle sidebar, and run it. You do not need the key first. The palette also shows each command's key beside it, so you learn the key as you go.

fixes.title: Use a viewer for the frontmost app
fixes.text: KeyCue displays the shortcuts of the app you are using. Its download page lists version 11.2.1, dated Aug 3, 2026, and macOS 13 or later. Check the price on the Ergonis site before you install. A viewer helps when you forget a key in the middle of work.

fixes.title: Ask Lazur what is on screen
fixes.text: Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask what a command does or where it is. Lazur answers out loud and points with a circle and a label. Confirm in the menu when the answer matters for a real action.

fixes.title: Check for clashes in one pane
fixes.text: A clash makes a shortcut do nothing or run the wrong command. Look in System Settings > Keyboard > Keyboard Shortcuts for system shortcuts that take the keys you want. Move your custom key to something no menu uses.

fixes.title: Keep a one-page sheet grouped by app
fixes.text: Write each shortcut next to its menu path, such as Edit > Find. The path rescues you when the key slips. Review the sheet every week and remove anything you no longer use.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Read the menus of your main app
plan.text: Open each top-level menu in your main app once. Read the symbols beside the commands. Pick three commands you use every week and write them down with their menu paths.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Practice with the mouse off
plan.text: Work for a short session using only the keys for those three commands. When you reach for the mouse, stop and find the key in the menu. Note which key slipped.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Add one App Shortcut
plan.text: Choose one menu command with no shortcut that you click often. Add it in System Settings > Keyboard > Keyboard Shortcuts > App Shortcuts. Type the exact menu name, then test it in the app.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Check for clashes
plan.text: If a key does nothing, look for a clash. Check the frontmost app first, then the Keyboard Shortcuts pane. Fix one clash and note what caused it.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Write your sheet
plan.text: Make a one-page note grouped by app. Put each menu path next to its key. Hold fn to dictate it if typing takes too long.

plan.label: Day 7
plan.title: Test yourself and cut
plan.text: Close the note and try each shortcut from memory. Keep the ones you still use. Remove the rest, then add the next three commands you reach for.
